title: Theories of Revolution
description: Skocpol, Tilly, Goldstone — why states collapse and movements seize power

concepts.title: What Counts as a Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
The scholarly study of revolutions distinguishes several related but distinct categories. Political revolutions change a country's government, often through unconstitutional means, but typically without restructuring the underlying social order — the 1688 English Glorious Revolution and the 1830 French July Revolution are canonical cases. Social revolutions in addition transform underlying class structures, property relations, and social hierarchies — the French Revolution of 1789–1799, the 1917 Russian Revolution, and the 1949 Chinese Revolution are the standard cases. Coups change leadership without mobilising mass participation; civil wars involve armed contestation between substantial factions; peaceful transitions achieve significant change without unconstitutional rupture.

The boundaries between these categories are contested. The 1979 Iranian Revolution combined social-revolutionary content with a religious framing that earlier theories had not anticipated. The 1989 East European revolutions had revolutionary speed and consequences but were largely peaceful and operated within (eventually) constitutional frameworks. The Arab Spring uprisings of 2010–2012 produced revolutionary outcomes in Tunisia and Egypt but mostly less-revolutionary outcomes elsewhere. The honest scholarly position is that 'revolution' is a family-resemblance category whose paradigmatic cases (1789, 1917) anchor a wider variation of cases that share some features.

The theoretical ambition of revolution-studies has always been to explain why some states collapse into revolutionary transformation while most do not. The literature has gone through several waves. The early-20th-century 'natural history of revolution' approach (Crane Brinton) emphasised stages — financial crisis, intellectual disaffection, transfer of allegiance of intellectuals, the moderate phase, the radical phase, the Thermidor reaction — common to multiple revolutionary cases. Subsequent waves have shifted toward more analytically structured accounts.

concepts.title: Skocpol and Structural Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
The most influential single theoretical framework for understanding revolutions is Theda Skocpol's States and Social Revolutions (1979). The book is a comparative-historical analysis of the French (1789), Russian (1917), and Chinese (1911–1949) revolutions, and it produced a structural account that displaced the earlier 'natural history' tradition.

Skocpol's central argument: social revolutions are not made by revolutionary movements through their own efforts; they happen despite revolutionary intentions, when specific structural conditions converge. The conditions she identified included: state crisis (typically driven by international military or economic pressure exceeding the state's capacity to respond); peasant capacity for collective action (variable across countries based on land tenure, rural community structure, and patterns of state-peasant relations); and marginal elite groups available to lead the revolutionary movement when central authority collapsed. The combination produced revolutionary outcomes; either factor alone produced lesser disruptions.

The framework has been criticised in detail. Skocpol's deliberate de-emphasis of ideology — her insistence that revolutions are made by structural conditions rather than by the ideas of revolutionaries — was contested by historians of the French and Russian revolutions for whom revolutionary ideology was clearly important. Her case selection (limited to social revolutions in agrarian-bureaucratic states) has been challenged by subsequent waves of work. But the structural-comparative approach has been generative, producing a substantial literature including Jeff Goodwin's No Other Way Out (2001), Charles Tilly's European Revolutions (1993), and Jack Goldstone's Revolution and Rebellion in the Early Modern World (1991).

concepts.title: Tilly, Goldstone, and Resource Mobilisation
concepts.contentHtml:
Charles Tilly's contribution to revolution theory shifted the analytical frame from the structural-conditions question to the resource mobilisation question. Tilly's argument: revolutions are large-scale instances of contentious politics, the broader category of collective action that includes social movements, riots, strikes, and rebellions. The conditions under which contentious politics escalates into revolution include the alignment of multiple sovereignty (rival claims to ultimate authority within a single political unit), broad coalitions across previously disconnected social groups, and state weakness reducing the cost of revolutionary commitment. Tilly's Mobilization to Revolution (1978) and subsequent work made the resource-mobilisation analysis the standard alternative to Skocpol's structural account.

Jack Goldstone's Revolution and Rebellion in the Early Modern World (1991) built on demographic-economic analysis. His argument: early-modern revolutionary upheavals (the English Civil War, the Fronde, the Ottoman Celali rebellions) all coincided with periods of population growth that exceeded agricultural and political-administrative capacity. Population pressure produced fiscal crisis, popular distress, elite competition for limited offices, and ideological crisis — the combination of which made revolutionary outcomes more likely. Goldstone's later Revolutions (2014) extended the analysis to modern cases.

The contemporary synthesis draws on multiple traditions. Modern revolution theory typically combines structural conditions (state crisis, fiscal stress, elite fragmentation), agency factors (revolutionary movements, ideologies, leadership), and contingent triggers (military defeats, economic crises, royal deaths). The relative weights vary by case. The honest assessment is that revolutions are sufficiently rare and contingent events that no single theoretical framework provides complete predictive power; the value of the literature is in identifying the recurring features that make revolutions more or less likely under specified conditions.

title: The English & American Revolutions
description: 1688 and 1776 — constitutional revolutions and the birth of modern republics

concepts.title: The English Revolutions
concepts.contentHtml:
England produced two consequential 17th-century revolutions. The English Civil War (1642–1651) was a complex multi-party conflict involving the Crown under Charles I, Parliament, and various social and religious factions. Parliament's victory in 1645–1646 led to the trial and execution of Charles I (1649), the Commonwealth and Protectorate under Oliver Cromwell (1653–1658), and substantial constitutional and religious upheaval. The episode produced both formal political-philosophical reflection (Hobbes's Leviathan, 1651, framing absolute sovereignty as necessary against civil war; the Levellers' Agreement of the People proposing radical constitutional reform) and lasting institutional changes — though the 1660 Stuart Restoration partially undid the political revolution.

The Glorious Revolution of 1688 produced the more durable settlement. The 1688–1689 deposition of James II and the accession of William III and Mary II (with formal constitutional limits) established Parliamentary supremacy as a permanent feature of British constitutional law. The 1689 Bill of Rights codified key features: parliamentary control of taxation, requirement of regular parliaments, freedom of debate, prohibition on standing armies in peacetime without parliamentary consent. The post-1688 constitutional settlement provided the framework for the subsequent development of British parliamentary democracy and influenced constitutional thinking across the Atlantic and beyond.

The intellectual consequence of the English revolutionary period was substantial. John Locke's Two Treatises of Government (1689) provided the canonical liberal defence of consent-based government and the right to resist tyrannical rule. The combination of practical institutional innovation with theoretical articulation of liberal-constitutional principles made the English seventeenth century one of the most influential periods in the intellectual history of modern politics.

concepts.title: The American Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
The American Revolution (1765–1789) emerged from the post-Seven-Years-War British attempts to recoup the costs of empire through colonial taxation. Key episodes included the Stamp Act crisis (1765), the Townshend duties (1767), the Boston Tea Party (1773), the Coercive Acts (1774), and the outbreak of armed conflict at Lexington and Concord (1775). The Declaration of Independence (July 1776) articulated the rebellion's political-philosophical foundations in terms drawn substantially from Locke. The 1781 Articles of Confederation produced the first US constitutional framework; the 1787 Constitution and the 1791 Bill of Rights produced the federal framework that has continued (with amendments) to the present.

The distinctive features of the American Revolution included its republican rather than monarchical-constitutional outcome, the construction of a federal system distributing power between national and state governments, the codification of constitutional limits and individual rights in a single written document with judicial enforcement, and the explicit articulation of consent-based government as the foundation of legitimate political authority. The combination influenced subsequent constitutional drafting from the French revolutionary period through to the post-1989 wave of new constitutions.

The Revolution's limits were also substantial. The constitution's accommodation of slavery — the three-fifths clause, the fugitive-slave clause, the federal protection of the slave trade until 1808 — embedded a contradiction that took the Civil War (1861–1865) and Reconstruction to begin to resolve. The exclusion of women, indigenous Americans, and free Black Americans from full political citizenship was not addressed by the founding generation. The scholarly debate over how to assess the revolution's character — radical or conservative, complete or incomplete, libertarian or republican — continues. Bernard Bailyn, Gordon Wood, Pauline Maier, Alan Taylor, Annette Gordon-Reed, and Sean Wilentz have all produced major contributions to the contemporary historiography.

concepts.title: Constitutional Revolutions and Their Influence
concepts.contentHtml:
The English and American revolutions shared a distinctive feature compared to subsequent revolutionary traditions: their outcomes were fundamentally constitutional rather than social-revolutionary. The 1688 settlement and the 1789 US Constitution did not seek to overthrow the underlying social order — they sought to establish institutional frameworks for self-government within the existing social structure. The contrast with the French Revolution's social-revolutionary ambitions (and the Russian and Chinese Revolutions' more radical social transformations) is one of the central typological distinctions in revolution studies.

The influence of the constitutional-revolution model has been enormous. Most subsequent democratic constitutional drafting has drawn on either or both. The French revolutionary constitutions, the post-1815 European liberal constitutional movements, the post-1860 Latin American constitutional traditions, the post-1945 reconstruction of European democracies, and the post-1989 Eastern European constitutional drafting all bear the marks of the Anglo-American constitutional inheritance.

The intellectual influence has been similarly substantial. The Federalist Papers (1787–1788), Locke's Second Treatise (1689), Madison's Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention (1787), and the broader corpus of late-18th-century Anglo-American constitutional thought continue to be central reference points in constitutional theory and democratic thought. The fact that the United States has continued to operate under its 1787 Constitution longer than any other written constitutional document — through civil war, depression, world wars, and substantial social transformation — is one of the most remarkable institutional facts of modern political history, even as the post-2010 stresses on US constitutional norms raise renewed questions about the framework's resilience.

title: The French Revolution
description: 1789, the Terror, Napoleon — the template for modern revolutionary politics

concepts.title: From Estates-General to Republic
concepts.contentHtml:
The French Revolution (1789–1799) produced the modern revolutionary template. The crisis began with the bankrupt French monarchy's 1789 calling of the Estates-General, a representative body that had not met since 1614. The Third Estate's (commoners') demand for one-man-one-vote rather than estate-by-estate voting, the formation of the National Assembly (June 17, 1789), the Tennis Court Oath (June 20), and the popular storming of the Bastille (July 14, 1789) initiated the revolutionary process.

The revolution's political phases moved through distinct constitutional structures. The National Constituent Assembly (1789–1791) produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (August 1789, the canonical statement of revolutionary principles), abolished feudal privileges (the Night of August 4–5, 1789), nationalised church property, and produced the 1791 Constitution establishing a constitutional monarchy. The Legislative Assembly (1791–1792) and the National Convention (1792–1795) presided over the September 1792 abolition of monarchy, the trial and execution of Louis XVI (January 1793), and the first French Republic.

The radical phase emerged during the Convention period. The Jacobin faction under Maximilien Robespierre dominated through the Committee of Public Safety from mid-1793 to mid-1794, conducting the Reign of Terror (September 1793 – July 1794) that executed an estimated 17,000 people through revolutionary tribunals plus another 10,000–25,000 in prison and through extra-judicial killings. The Terror's combination of revolutionary idealism with mass political violence has been one of the most studied and most contested episodes in modern political history.

concepts.title: Thermidor, Directory, and Napoleon
concepts.contentHtml:
The Terror's end came with the Thermidorian Reaction (July 27, 1794, 9 Thermidor in the revolutionary calendar). Robespierre and his closest allies were arrested and executed within days. The subsequent post-Thermidor government — the Convention's revised composition through to October 1795, then the Directory of 1795–1799 — pulled back from radical revolutionary measures while preserving the major institutional changes of 1789–1791. The Directory's combination of corruption, military overstretch, and political instability set the stage for the next phase.

Napoleon Bonaparte's November 9, 1799 coup (18 Brumaire) ended the Directory and established the Consulate. Napoleon's subsequent transformation of the French state — the 1804 Civil Code, the centralised administrative system, the meritocratic appointment of officials, the Concordat of 1801 with the papacy, the systematic reorganisation of the legal and educational systems — institutionalised many of the revolution's modernising goals while abandoning its democratic and republican aspirations. The 1804 declaration of empire formalised the rejection of republican forms; the subsequent military campaigns took Napoleonic legal and administrative innovations across most of continental Europe.

The 1815 defeat at Waterloo ended Napoleon's rule but did not undo the revolution's institutional changes. The Bourbon Restoration (1815–1830) operated within constitutional limits unimaginable to the pre-1789 monarchy. The 1830 July Revolution, the 1848 February Revolution, and the various subsequent French regime changes worked through the institutional vocabulary the revolution had created. The cumulative effect was to make the 1789 revolution the modern reference point for revolutionary politics — its categories (left, right, ancien régime, citizen, the people, the nation, revolution itself) became the standard vocabulary for political conflict for the next two centuries.

concepts.title: Interpretations and Legacies
concepts.contentHtml:
The interpretation of the French Revolution has been one of the central battlegrounds of modern political thought. The liberal-Whig tradition (the post-1789 European liberal movements, John Stuart Mill) emphasised the revolution's constitutional and rights-based achievements while criticising the Terror's violence. The conservative tradition (Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790) provided the foundational critique of revolutionary abstraction, emphasising the value of inherited institutions and the dangers of rationalist reconstruction. The Marxist tradition (Marx, Engels, and successors) read 1789 as the bourgeois revolution that established capitalism, with the proletarian revolution still to come. The republican tradition emphasised the revolution's democratic and citizenship-based achievements as the foundation of modern political legitimacy.

The 20th-century historiography produced major reinterpretations. Albert Mathiez and Georges Lefebvre's social-historical accounts emphasised peasant and urban-popular participation. François Furet's Penser la Révolution française (1978, English 1981) launched a revisionist tradition that displaced the Marxist orthodoxy in French academic historiography, emphasising the discursive and ideological dimensions of revolutionary politics. Lynn Hunt, Keith Baker, and others have continued the cultural-historical reinterpretation.

The contemporary legacy is substantial. The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man remains a foundational reference for human-rights documents (it is incorporated by reference into the current French constitution). The political vocabulary of left and right derives from the seating arrangement in the 1789 National Assembly. The very category of revolutionary politics — that mass mobilisation can transform basic institutions through deliberate political action — was substantially shaped by the French case. Whether the next phase of contemporary politics will produce comparable revolutionary transformations or will operate within the post-1989 constitutional frameworks is one of the open questions of the period.

title: Russian & Chinese Revolutions
description: 1917 and 1949 — peasant revolution and the communist project

concepts.title: The Russian Revolution of 1917
concepts.contentHtml:
The Russian Revolution of 1917 was actually two related events. The February Revolution (February 23 – March 3, 1917 in the Julian calendar; March 8–16 in the Gregorian) emerged from food shortages, working-class strikes in Petrograd, and the collapse of the Tsarist autocracy under the strain of the First World War. Tsar Nicholas II abdicated; the Provisional Government under Prince Lvov (then Alexander Kerensky from July) attempted a constitutional democratic transition.

The October Revolution (October 24–25 Julian / November 6–7 Gregorian) was the Bolshevik seizure of power. Vladimir Lenin's small but disciplined Bolshevik party, transported to Russia from Swiss exile by German military authorities seeking to destabilise the Eastern Front, exploited the Provisional Government's weakness. Through control of the Petrograd Soviet, the slogan 'Peace, Bread, Land,' and a tactical insurrection, the Bolsheviks took power and established the Soviet government. The Russian Civil War (1918–1922) consolidated Bolshevik control through what came to be called War Communism.

Lenin's death in 1924 and Joseph Stalin's subsequent consolidation of power produced one of the 20th century's most distinctive political regimes. The collectivisation of agriculture (1929–1933) destroyed the kulak class through forced settlement; the resulting Holodomor famine in Ukraine and other grain-producing regions killed an estimated 4–7 million people, most controversially recognised as a genocide by various contemporary governments. The Great Terror of 1936–1938 executed perhaps 700,000 people through political purges and imprisoned millions in the Gulag system. The combination of forced industrialisation, mass political repression, and ideological orthodoxy produced the regime that survived the Second World War, expanded into Eastern Europe, and contested the Cold War with the United States until its 1991 collapse.

concepts.title: The Chinese Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
The Chinese Revolution was a longer and more complicated process than its Russian predecessor. The 1911 Xinhai Revolution ended the Qing dynasty and produced the Republic of China under Sun Yat-sen and (later) Yuan Shikai. The subsequent Warlord Era (1916–1928) saw fragmented military rule across China; the Nationalist (Kuomintang) reunification under Chiang Kai-shek produced nominal unity from 1928 to 1937 but did not consolidate state authority across the country.

The Chinese Communist Party (CCP), founded in Shanghai in 1921 with Soviet support, struggled in its early decades. The 1927 Shanghai Massacre, in which Chiang turned on his Communist allies, drove the CCP into rural exile. The 1934–1935 Long March took Mao Zedong's faction from Jiangxi to Yan'an across 6,000 miles, establishing the leadership and ideological foundations that would later govern the People's Republic. The Japanese invasion (1937–1945) reshaped the Chinese political landscape; the post-war Civil War (1945–1949) produced the CCP victory and the establishment of the People's Republic of China on October 1, 1949.

The PRC's early decades produced two especially destructive episodes. The Great Leap Forward (1958–1962), Mao's attempt to industrialise rapidly through commune-based agriculture and backyard steel production, produced the largest famine in human history — an estimated 30–45 million deaths over four years. The Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) was Mao's mobilisation of youth and Red Guard movements against the party's bureaucratic establishment; the political violence killed an estimated 1–2 million and disrupted Chinese institutions, education, and cultural life for a generation. Deng Xiaoping's post-1978 reform programme initiated the transformation of China from Maoist socialism to market-Leninist authoritarianism that has produced the world's second-largest economy and the continuing CCP one-party state.

concepts.title: Communist Revolutions: Lessons and Legacies
concepts.contentHtml:
The 20th-century communist revolutions raise enduring questions about revolutionary politics. The scholarship on what went wrong has been extensive. Stéphane Courtois et al's Black Book of Communism (1997) compiled estimates of communist regime deaths globally at around 100 million, a contested but influential figure. Robert Conquest's long career documented the Soviet purges, famines, and Gulag in detail. Frank Dikötter's trilogy on Mao-era China has produced one of the most thorough scholarly accounts of the Great Leap Forward famine. The pattern of revolutionary movements that promised liberation producing instead concentrated political power and mass death has been one of the central historical lessons of the 20th century.

The theoretical debate continues. The orthodox Marxist response was that the Russian and Chinese cases were not real socialism but distortions; the post-1989 collapse of state-socialist regimes substantially undermined that defence. The contemporary defence of socialist politics, when it engages with this history, typically emphasises democratic-socialist rather than vanguard-revolutionary lineages. The liberal critique emphasises the structural problems of vanguard revolutionary politics — the temptation to consolidate power against counterrevolutionary threats, the difficulty of distinguishing genuine threats from political opposition, the absence of institutional checks on revolutionary leadership.

The practical legacy in contemporary geopolitics is substantial. China's continued one-party state, North Korea's hereditary communist regime, Vietnam's Communist Party (with its post-1986 economic reforms), Cuba's continuing Castroist state, and Laos's continuing Lao People's Revolutionary Party all trace lineages to the 20th-century communist revolutions. The post-1989 transformations of formerly-communist states — to varying mixes of liberal democracy, illiberal democracy, and authoritarian backsliding — illustrate the continued political consequences of the revolutionary periods. Whether the post-1991 'end of history' liberal optimism about post-communist transitions has been supported by the subsequent evidence is one of the major political-economy assessments of the contemporary period; the answer is mostly no.

title: 20th Century Liberation Movements
description: Anti-colonial, civil rights, feminist movements — politics from below

concepts.title: Anti-Colonial Liberation
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-1945 wave of anti-colonial liberation movements produced the most extensive single-period decolonisation in human history. The combination of European wartime exhaustion, Cold War ideological pressure, UN principles, and decades of organised nationalist mobilisation produced the dismantling of the British, French, Dutch, Belgian, and Portuguese empires within roughly thirty years. The earlier lesson on decolonisation covers the institutional dimensions; the present lesson focuses on the liberation movements' political and ideological characters.

Major liberation movements developed distinct intellectual frameworks. Mahatma Gandhi's leadership of the Indian National Congress combined mass civil disobedience (the 1930 Salt March; the Quit India movement of 1942) with explicit philosophical commitments to nonviolence (satyagraha) and inter-religious cooperation. The Indian independence model influenced subsequent movements globally. Frantz Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth (1961) articulated the theoretical framework for armed anti-colonial struggle, drawing on his clinical experience in Algeria and on Hegelian-Marxist categories. The contrast between Gandhian nonviolence and Fanonian armed struggle continues to structure debates about resistance strategy.

The specific liberation movements varied substantially. The Algerian FLN's eight-year war (1954–1962) produced the bloodiest decolonisation conflict in Africa and reshaped both Algerian and French politics for a generation. The Vietminh (later succeeded by other Vietnamese revolutionary organisations) fought first the French, then the Americans, in a 30-year war producing perhaps 3 million Vietnamese deaths, alongside some 58,000 American and several thousand South Korean and other allied deaths. The African National Congress's eventual triumph in South Africa came in 1994, after decades of armed struggle and diplomatic-isolation campaigns. The post-independence trajectories of these movements — varying from democratic consolidation through various forms of single-party rule and authoritarianism — illustrate how successful liberation does not automatically produce successful post-liberation governance.

concepts.title: Civil Rights and the Struggle for Equality
concepts.contentHtml:
The American civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s produced one of the most successful single mass-mobilisation campaigns in modern political history. The post-1945 sequence — Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956), the Little Rock crisis (1957), the sit-in movement (1960), the Freedom Rides (1961), the Birmingham Campaign (1963), the March on Washington (1963), the Selma to Montgomery marches (1965) — combined legal litigation, nonviolent direct action, and mass mobilisation to produce the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

The movement's intellectual leadership included Martin Luther King Jr. (whose 'Letter from Birmingham Jail,' 1963, is among the most-cited documents of postwar American political thought), Bayard Rustin, Ella Baker, John Lewis, and many others. King's combination of African-American Christian preaching tradition, Gandhian nonviolence, and explicit theological-political commitments produced one of the most successful single political-rhetorical traditions in the modern democratic world.

The limits of the civil rights movement and the subsequent Black Power movement of the late 1960s and 1970s illustrate the tension between integrationist and self-determination strands within Black American politics. The post-1968 fragmentation, the 1970s economic transformations that affected Black industrial-working-class communities, the post-1980 mass-incarceration wave, and the persistent racial inequality across multiple metrics indicate that civil rights victories did not produce racial equality. The 21st-century resurgence of mass mobilisation around racial justice (Black Lives Matter from 2013, the post-2020 protest wave) draws on the civil rights inheritance while also acknowledging its limits.

concepts.title: Feminism, Gay Liberation, and Identity-Based Movements
concepts.contentHtml:
The 20th-century feminist movement developed in waves with distinctive intellectual and political characters. First-wave feminism (roughly 1840s–1920s) focused on legal equality, particularly women's suffrage — achieved progressively from New Zealand 1893 through to most major democracies by the early 20th century. Second-wave feminism (1960s–1980s) extended the analysis to workplace equality, reproductive rights, domestic violence, and broader cultural patterns; major intellectual texts included Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex (1949) and Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963). Third-wave feminism (1990s–) and subsequent feminist work has emphasised intersectionality, transgender inclusion, global perspectives, and the political-economy of gendered labour.

The gay liberation movement took the Stonewall riots of June 1969 as its iconic founding moment. The subsequent half-century has produced one of the most rapid social-political transformations in modern history: the decriminalisation of homosexuality across most democratic countries, the expansion of anti-discrimination law, the achievement of marriage equality in over 30 countries, and the increasing visibility of trans and non-binary identities. The backlash to LGBTQ+ rights has been substantial in several countries (Russia, Hungary, the post-2024 US administrative changes, anti-LGBTQ+ legislation in multiple African states), illustrating that the movement's gains are not unconditional or universal.

The broader pattern of identity-based liberation movements — disability rights, indigenous rights, immigrant rights, environmental justice — has been one of the central features of late-20th and early-21st century politics. The combination of legal-litigation strategies, mass mobilisation, intellectual articulation, and (increasingly) digital-platform organisation has produced an extensive set of political infrastructure for identity-based mobilisation. The continuing question of how these movements relate to broader democratic-political coalitions, how they manage internal disagreement, and how they sustain themselves across generations is one of the central practical-political questions of contemporary movement organising.

title: Color Revolutions & the Arab Spring
description: Post-1989 democratic uprisings — successes, betrayals, and counter-revolutions

concepts.title: 1989 and the Velvet Revolutions
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-1989 wave of Eastern European democratic revolutions was one of the most consequential single political transformations of the 20th century. The combination of Gorbachev's Soviet reforms (glasnost from 1985, perestroika), the Polish Round Table negotiations (early 1989), the Hungarian opening of the Austrian border, the East German exodus and the November 9, 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall, the Czechoslovak Velvet Revolution (November 17 – December 29, 1989), and the more violent Romanian revolution against Ceaușescu (December 1989) produced the collapse of communist regimes across the Warsaw Pact within months.

The 1989 transformations had distinctive features. They were largely peaceful (Romania was the major exception). They operated through negotiation (the Polish Round Table model) where possible. They produced constitutional rather than purely revolutionary outcomes — most successor states adopted new constitutional frameworks within months, restoring liberal-democratic institutions or attempting to. The combination earned the label 'refolution' (revolution and reform together) from the British political scientist Timothy Garton Ash.

The 1991 dissolution of the Soviet Union followed a similar pattern through different political processes. The August 1991 hardliner coup attempt against Gorbachev failed within three days; Yeltsin's successful resistance accelerated the process; the Belovezha Accords (December 1991) formally dissolved the Soviet Union into 15 successor states. The subsequent post-Soviet trajectories diverged dramatically — the Baltic states consolidated as liberal democracies and EU members, Russia under Yeltsin then Putin moved through liberal-then-illiberal-then-authoritarian forms, the Central Asian republics produced authoritarian-presidential regimes, and Belarus moved into the Lukashenko one-party authoritarianism that has persisted since 1994.

concepts.title: Color Revolutions in the Post-Soviet Space
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-2000 'color revolutions' applied the 1989 model to several post-Soviet states. The Rose Revolution in Georgia (November 2003) deposed Eduard Shevardnadze through mass protests after disputed parliamentary elections; Mikheil Saakashvili came to power and pursued substantial reforms. The Orange Revolution in Ukraine (November 2004 – January 2005) overturned a fraudulent presidential election and installed Viktor Yushchenko. The Tulip Revolution in Kyrgyzstan (March 2005) deposed Askar Akayev. The Cedar Revolution in Lebanon (February–April 2005) forced the withdrawal of Syrian troops after the Hariri assassination.

The color revolutions had common features. They were triggered by fraudulent elections; they used mass protest in capital cities; they were largely peaceful; they had international support (Western democracy-promotion organisations, EU institutions, US-funded NGOs); they used distinctive symbols (colors, flowers) to coordinate participation. The model became widely studied — both as a successful template for democratic transition and as a Russian-government object of suspicion (Putin's identification of the color revolutions as Western-engineered conspiracies has shaped Russian foreign policy throughout the post-2003 period).

The medium-term outcomes have been mixed. Georgia's post-Saakashvili period has produced both reform success and political instability. Ukraine's post-Orange-Revolution period saw substantial political failure followed by the 2014 Euromaidan (the Revolution of Dignity, November 2013 – February 2014) that overthrew Yanukovych and triggered the Russian invasion of Crimea and the Donbas. Kyrgyzstan has had multiple subsequent revolutions and remains politically unstable. Lebanon's political system has continued to dysfunction. The pattern across cases: revolutionary success at deposing specific leaders did not always produce the institutional transformation needed for durable liberal-democratic outcomes.

concepts.title: The Arab Spring and Its Aftermath
concepts.contentHtml:
The Arab Spring uprisings of 2010–2012 represented the largest single mass-mobilisation movement in the post-1989 period. The catalyst was Mohamed Bouazizi's December 17, 2010 self-immolation in Tunisia in protest of police harassment. The Tunisian Revolution deposed Ben Ali within weeks (January 2011); subsequent protests spread to Egypt (the 18-day Tahrir Square mobilisation that deposed Mubarak in February 2011), Libya (which descended into civil war and the Western-backed overthrow of Gaddafi), Yemen (a contested transition that eventually produced civil war), Bahrain (suppressed by Saudi-led intervention), Syria (which descended into one of the 21st century's most destructive civil wars), and protest movements of varying intensity across the broader region.

The outcomes were largely disappointing. Tunisia produced the only relatively successful democratic transition for a decade, though backsliding under Kais Saied since 2021 has eroded democratic institutions. Egypt produced a brief democratic interlude under Mohamed Morsi before the 2013 military coup under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi reinstated authoritarian rule. Libya, Syria, and Yemen produced sustained civil wars with hundreds of thousands of deaths, mass displacement, and extensive regional and international intervention. Bahrain, Jordan, Morocco, and other monarchies maintained their pre-Arab-Spring regimes through varying combinations of repression and limited reform.

The scholarly assessment of why the Arab Spring largely failed has produced rich literature. Common themes include: the absence of pre-existing democratic institutions, the role of military and intelligence services in shaping outcomes, the geopolitical interventions of regional and international powers, the religious-secular cleavages that fractured opposition coalitions, and the economic-stagnation conditions that produced the original protests but were not addressed by post-transition governments. The combination has produced widespread pessimism about prospects for democratic transition in the region, and contributed to the broader post-2010 narrative of democratic recession globally. Whether the recent (2024) Bangladeshi uprising, Sri Lankan protests, and other contemporary mobilisations represent a new democratic-revolutionary wave or another partially-failed cycle is one of the open questions of the contemporary period.
